Topics.Title: Overview of Module Creation in PreseMaker
Topics.Summary: Introduces the concept of modules in PreseMaker and explains why there are multiple ways to create them. Sets the stage for understanding when and why each method is used.

Elements.Title: What Is a Module in PreseMaker?
Elements.BodyText: A module is the fundamental unit of content in PreseMaker, representing a self-contained learning or presentation package that can be built, managed, and deployed independently.
Elements.Notes: Think of a module as a project folder that holds all the assets, settings, and generated content for a single topic or course unit.

Items.Text: Each module contains its own configuration, source materials, and output content, keeping projects organized and portable.
Modules can be created from scratch, sourced from existing work on disk, or brought in from an external file or repository.
Understanding what a module is provides the foundation for choosing the right creation method for any given situation.

Elements.Title: Why Multiple Creation Methods Exist
Elements.BodyText: PreseMaker offers three distinct methods for creating a module because different workflows and starting points call for different approaches.
Elements.Notes: Having multiple methods prevents a one-size-fits-all bottleneck and accommodates teams working in varied environments — from solo authors starting fresh to teams sharing pre-built modules.

Items.Text: A new AI-generated module suits authors who are starting from scratch and want PreseMaker to scaffold the structure automatically.
Adding an existing folder from disk is ideal when content has already been organized locally and simply needs to be registered with PreseMaker.
Importing from a file or repository supports collaboration and reuse, allowing modules built elsewhere to be brought into the current workspace.

Elements.Title: The Role of the Module Manager
Elements.BodyText: The Module Manager is the central hub in PreseMaker through which all module creation and management actions are initiated and tracked.
Elements.Notes: Learners will interact with the Module Manager at the start of every module workflow, making familiarity with its interface essential before exploring individual creation methods.

Items.Text: The Module Manager provides a unified view of all modules currently available in the workspace.
It guides users from an empty or newly registered module through to a state where content generation can begin.
All three creation methods are accessible directly from within the Module Manager, keeping the workflow consistent regardless of the approach chosen.

Elements.Title: Setting the Stage: From Empty to Ready
Elements.BodyText: Regardless of which creation method is used, the end goal is the same — bringing a module to a 'ready' state where PreseMaker can generate or display content.
Elements.Notes: The concept of a module moving through states (empty → configured → ready) is a key mental model that applies across all three methods covered in this lesson.

Items.Text: A newly created module starts in an empty or minimal state and must be configured before content generation is possible.
The Module Manager signals when a module has met the requirements needed to proceed to content generation.
Understanding this progression helps learners recognize what each creation method accomplishes and what steps remain after the module is created.

Elements.Title: Choosing the Right Method: A Preview
Elements.BodyText: Selecting the appropriate creation method depends on where your starting materials are, how the module was originally produced, and how your team collaborates.
Elements.Notes: This topic sets the stage for deeper dives into each method; learners should leave with a clear sense that method choice is deliberate and context-driven, not arbitrary.

Items.Text: Authors beginning a brand-new project with no prior assets will typically reach for the AI generation method.
Those who have previously organized content in a local folder structure can add that folder directly, preserving their existing organization.
Teams sharing modules across systems or pulling from a version-controlled repository will rely on the import method to bring external modules into their local environment.

Topics.Title: Method 1: Generating a New Module with AI
Topics.Summary: Covers how to use PreseMaker's AI-powered generation feature to create a brand-new module from scratch. Learners explore the inputs required and what the AI produces as output.

Elements.Title: Overview of AI-Powered Module Generation
Elements.BodyText: PreseMaker's AI generation feature allows learners to create a brand-new module from scratch without any pre-existing files or content.
Elements.Notes: This method is ideal for users starting a project with no prior materials, relying entirely on AI to scaffold the module structure.

Items.Text: AI generation is one of three available methods for creating a module in PreseMaker.
The feature is designed to reduce manual setup by automating the initial structure and content outline of the module.
This approach is best suited when no existing module folder or importable file is available.

Elements.Title: Accessing the AI Generation Option
Elements.BodyText: Learners initiate AI-powered module creation through the Module Manager, which serves as the central hub for all module creation methods.
Elements.Notes: The Module Manager presents all three creation methods, and selecting the AI generation option leads the user into the input collection workflow.

Items.Text: The Module Manager is the starting point where users choose between generating, adding, or importing a module.
Selecting the AI generation method launches a guided input process within the Module Manager interface.

Elements.Title: Required Inputs for AI Generation
Elements.BodyText: Before the AI can generate a module, users must supply specific inputs that guide the content and structure of the output.
Elements.Notes: The quality and specificity of the inputs directly influence the relevance and accuracy of the AI-generated module.

Items.Text: Users provide a module title, a description, and one or more source materials (for example a document, web page, PowerPoint, pasted text, or YouTube transcript).
These inputs act as parameters that shape the AI's understanding of the desired module scope and depth.
Providing clear and detailed inputs helps the AI produce a more accurate and usable module structure.

Elements.Title: What the AI Produces as Output
Elements.BodyText: Once the required inputs are submitted, PreseMaker's AI generates a structured module ready to be reviewed and built upon.
Elements.Notes: The generated output is not final content but rather a scaffold that the user can refine further within the Module Manager.

Items.Text: The AI output typically includes a module title, description, and an organized set of topics or sections.
The generated structure serves as a starting framework, which learners can then populate with detailed content.
The output positions the module as 'ready for content generation,' representing a defined but editable foundation.

Elements.Title: From Empty Module to Content-Ready State
Elements.BodyText: The AI generation method guides users through a progression from an empty module to one that is structured and ready for further content development.
Elements.Notes: This progression is a key outcome emphasized in the Module Manager workflow for the AI generation path.

Items.Text: An empty module has no structure, topics, or content; the AI generation process fills this gap automatically.
Once generation is complete, the module transitions to a content-ready state where detailed authoring can begin.
The Module Manager tracks and reflects this progression, signaling when the module is prepared for the next stage.

Topics.Title: Method 2: Adding an Existing Module Folder from Disk
Topics.Summary: Explains how to bring a pre-existing module folder stored locally on disk into PreseMaker. Covers the steps and requirements for the folder to be recognized correctly.

Elements.Title: Overview of Method 2: Adding from Disk
Elements.BodyText: This method allows you to bring a pre-existing module folder that is already stored locally on your computer into PreseMaker without creating anything new from scratch.
Elements.Notes: This is useful when you have previously worked on a module outside of PreseMaker or received a module folder from a colleague.

Items.Text: The module folder must already exist on your local disk before you begin this process.
PreseMaker will reference the folder's location rather than duplicating its contents.
This method is ideal for resuming work on a module that was started in a previous session or on another machine.

Elements.Title: Locating the Existing Module Folder
Elements.BodyText: Before adding the folder, you must know the exact location of the module folder on your disk.
Elements.Notes: Use your operating system's file explorer to verify the folder path and confirm the folder contains the expected contents before proceeding.

Items.Text: Navigate to the directory on your disk where the module folder is stored.
Confirm the folder is accessible and not locked, hidden, or stored on a disconnected drive.
Note the full folder path, as you will need to provide it to PreseMaker during the import step.

Elements.Title: Folder Structure Requirements
Elements.BodyText: For PreseMaker to correctly recognize an existing folder as a valid module, the folder must meet certain structural requirements.
Elements.Notes: A folder that does not meet these requirements may not be recognized by PreseMaker, or it may be recognized but lack the data needed for content generation.

Items.Text: The folder must contain the expected PreseMaker module files or configuration markers that identify it as a module.
Subfolders and key files must follow the naming conventions PreseMaker uses internally.
Incomplete or corrupted folders may cause errors during the recognition process.

Elements.Title: Adding the Folder Through the Module Manager
Elements.BodyText: The Module Manager is the central interface used to add an existing folder from disk into PreseMaker.
Elements.Notes: The Module Manager guides you step by step, ensuring the folder is validated before it is fully loaded into the application.

Items.Text: Open the Module Manager within PreseMaker to access the option for adding an existing module from disk.
Use the provided browse or path-entry control to select or type the location of your module folder.
Once the folder path is submitted, PreseMaker will scan and validate the folder before making it available.

Elements.Title: Validation and Recognition by PreseMaker
Elements.BodyText: After pointing PreseMaker to the folder, the application performs a validation check to confirm the folder qualifies as a recognizable module.
Elements.Notes: If validation fails, PreseMaker will typically display an error or warning message indicating what is missing or incorrect.

Items.Text: PreseMaker checks for required files and structural elements during validation.
A successfully recognized folder will appear as a module entry within the Module Manager.
If the folder passes validation, you can proceed to work with the module as if it had been created natively in PreseMaker.

Elements.Title: Next Steps After Adding the Folder
Elements.BodyText: Once the existing folder is successfully added and recognized, it becomes available in PreseMaker for further editing and content generation.
Elements.Notes: At this stage, the module transitions from simply being a folder on disk to an active module within the PreseMaker environment.

Items.Text: The module will appear in the Module Manager list alongside any other modules you have created or imported.
You can open the module and review its existing content before making any changes.
From this point, the module is ready to be used with PreseMaker's content generation tools.

Topics.Title: Method 3: Importing from a File or Repository
Topics.Summary: Describes how to import a module using a file or a remote repository source. Highlights the scenarios where this method is most appropriate and the steps involved.

Elements.Title: What Is the Import Method?
Elements.BodyText: Importing from a file or repository is the third method for creating a module in PreseMaker, allowing users to bring in a module that already exists outside the current workspace.
Elements.Notes: This method is distinct from adding an existing folder from disk — it is designed for packaged files or remotely hosted sources.

Items.Text: This approach is ideal when a module has been shared as a packaged file or hosted in a remote repository.
It allows teams to reuse and distribute modules across different installations or environments.
No manual folder navigation is required; PreseMaker handles the intake process through the import workflow.

Elements.Title: When to Use This Method
Elements.BodyText: The import method is most appropriate in specific scenarios where the module source is not a local folder already on disk.
Elements.Notes: Choosing the right method depends on where the module originates and how it was packaged or shared.

Items.Text: Use this method when a colleague has sent you a packaged module file for reuse or review.
It is also the correct choice when pulling a module from a remote repository, such as a shared team or organizational source.
This method is preferred over the folder method when the module has not yet been extracted or placed in a local directory.

Elements.Title: Supported Source Types
Elements.BodyText: PreseMaker supports two distinct source types for this import method: a local packaged file and a remote repository URL.
Elements.Notes: Understanding which source type applies to your situation will determine how you proceed through the import steps.

Items.Text: A file-based import uses a packaged module archive stored on your computer or network drive.
A repository-based import points PreseMaker to a remote location, such as a hosted repository, from which the module is retrieved.
Both source types ultimately result in the module being registered and available within the Module Manager.

Elements.Title: Steps to Import a Module
Elements.BodyText: The import process follows a guided sequence within PreseMaker to ensure the module is correctly ingested and ready for use.
Elements.Notes: Following the steps in order prevents import errors and ensures the module is fully configured after intake.

Items.Text: Open the Module Manager and select the option to import a module from a file or repository.
Choose your source type — file or repository — and provide the required path or URL.
PreseMaker validates and processes the source, then registers the module so it appears in the Module Manager.
Once imported, the module is available for content generation or further editing just like any other module.

Elements.Title: Role of the Module Manager in This Method
Elements.BodyText: The Module Manager serves as the central hub for initiating and completing the import process, providing the interface and feedback needed throughout.
Elements.Notes: The Module Manager's consistent role across all three methods makes it the single point of reference for module creation and management.

Items.Text: All import actions are initiated from within the Module Manager, keeping the workflow centralized.
The Module Manager displays status and confirmation once the import is successfully completed.
After import, the module transitions from an empty or external state to one that is ready for content generation within PreseMaker.

Topics.Title: The Module Manager: Central Hub for Module Setup
Topics.Summary: Introduces the Module Manager interface as the central workspace that organizes and guides users through module creation. Explains how it tracks module status from empty to content-ready.

Elements.Title: What Is the Module Manager?
Elements.BodyText: The Module Manager is the central workspace in PreseMaker where all module creation and setup activities are organized and managed.
Elements.Notes: Think of it as a dashboard that keeps every module you work on visible and accessible in one place.

Items.Text: The Module Manager serves as the primary interface users interact with when starting, tracking, or configuring any module.
It consolidates all module-related actions so users do not need to navigate away to separate screens during setup.
Accessing the Module Manager is typically the first step after launching PreseMaker and deciding to work with a module.

Elements.Title: Organizing Modules Within the Manager
Elements.BodyText: The Module Manager displays all current modules in a structured layout, giving users a clear overview of what exists and what still needs attention.
Elements.Notes: This organizational view is especially useful when working on multiple modules simultaneously or returning to a project after a break.

Items.Text: Each module appears as a distinct entry, allowing users to quickly locate and select the one they want to work on.
The layout helps users distinguish between modules at different stages of completion at a glance.
Users can manage several modules from the same interface without losing context.

Elements.Title: Tracking Module Status: Empty to Content-Ready
Elements.BodyText: One of the Module Manager's key functions is tracking the lifecycle status of each module, from its initial empty state to being fully ready for content generation.
Elements.Notes: Status indicators guide users on what actions are still needed before a module can proceed to content generation.

Items.Text: A newly created module begins in an 'empty' status, signaling that no content or configuration has been added yet.
As users complete setup steps, the Module Manager updates the module's status to reflect its progress.
The final status state indicates the module is content-ready, meaning it is prepared for AI generation or further authoring.

Elements.Title: Guiding Users Through the Setup Process
Elements.BodyText: The Module Manager acts as a guide, helping users understand what steps are required to move a module from creation to readiness.
Elements.Notes: This guided approach reduces confusion for new users who may be unfamiliar with the full setup workflow.

Items.Text: The interface surfaces the necessary actions at each stage so users always know what to do next.
Setup milestones are made visible within the manager, reducing the chance of skipping a required configuration step.
Whether starting from AI generation, an existing folder, or an import, the Module Manager provides a consistent workflow path.

Elements.Title: Supporting All Three Creation Methods
Elements.BodyText: The Module Manager serves as the unified hub regardless of which of the three creation methods a user chooses to start a module.
Elements.Notes: This consistency means users only need to learn one interface to manage modules created through any available method.

Items.Text: Modules generated with AI, added from disk, or imported from a file or repository all appear and are managed within the same Module Manager interface.
The manager normalizes the experience so that post-creation steps are handled identically no matter how the module originated.
Users can mix modules from different creation methods and manage them side by side without any difference in workflow.

Topics.Title: From Empty Module to Content-Ready: The Module Lifecycle
Topics.Summary: Walks learners through the progression a module follows after creation, ending at the point where it is ready for content generation. Reinforces how the Module Manager supports each stage of this lifecycle.

Elements.Title: The Starting Point: An Empty Module
Elements.BodyText: A newly AI-generated module starts empty and needs its topics generated first; modules added from an existing folder or imported may already contain topics and content.
Elements.Notes: The starting point depends on the method: an AI-generated module must have its topics generated before it is ready, while an added or imported module may already include them.

Items.Text: An empty module contains the necessary structure but holds no generated content yet.
An AI-generated module begins with no topics and must have them generated; an added or imported module may already include topics and content.

Elements.Title: Introducing the Module Manager as Lifecycle Hub
Elements.BodyText: The Module Manager serves as the central interface that tracks and supports a module through every stage of its lifecycle after creation.
Elements.Notes: Think of the Module Manager as a dashboard that always reflects the current state of the module and surfaces the actions available at that stage.

Items.Text: Rather than navigating multiple separate tools, learners work within the Module Manager to move a module forward.
The Module Manager provides visibility into where a module currently sits in its lifecycle and what steps remain.
All three creation methods ultimately deposit the new module into the Module Manager for continued management.

Elements.Title: Progressing Through Lifecycle Stages
Elements.BodyText: After creation, a module passes through a defined sequence of stages before it is ready for content generation.
Elements.Notes: In practice the key requirement is simply that a module has a generated Topics list before most content can be generated from it.

Items.Text: Each stage represents a distinct readiness level, signaling what has been completed and what still needs to happen.
The Module Manager visually reflects the current stage so learners always know where the module stands.
Most content generation becomes available once the module has a generated Topics list.

Elements.Title: The Role of Configuration in the Lifecycle
Elements.BodyText: Between creation and content readiness, a module typically requires configuration steps that establish the parameters needed for content generation.
Elements.Notes: Configuration might include setting the module title, defining scope, or confirming source material — depending on which creation method was used.

Items.Text: Configuration steps ensure the module has sufficient context for PreseMaker to generate meaningful content.
The Module Manager guides learners through required configuration by surfacing relevant options at the appropriate lifecycle stage.
Skipping or incomplete configuration keeps a module from advancing to the content-ready state.

Elements.Title: Reaching the Content-Ready State
Elements.BodyText: The content-ready state is the final stage of the module lifecycle covered in this topic, representing the point at which content generation can begin.
Elements.Notes: Reaching content-ready is a milestone — it confirms that the module is properly structured and configured, and that PreseMaker has everything it needs to proceed.

Items.Text: A module in the content-ready state has passed through all prerequisite lifecycle stages successfully.
The Module Manager clearly indicates when a module has reached content-ready status, distinguishing it from modules still in earlier stages.
Once content-ready, the module is handed off to the content generation process — which is covered in subsequent lessons.

Elements.Title: How the Module Manager Reinforces Each Stage
Elements.BodyText: The Module Manager does not simply display lifecycle status passively — it actively supports learners by surfacing the right actions and information at each stage.
Elements.Notes: This design reduces errors and confusion by preventing out-of-sequence actions and making the next required step obvious at all times.

Items.Text: At each stage, the Module Manager highlights available actions while suppressing options that are not yet applicable.
Status indicators and progress cues within the Module Manager help learners build an accurate mental model of the lifecycle.
Consistent use of the Module Manager across all three creation methods reinforces a unified workflow regardless of how a module was originally created.
